title: Silas and the Language
premise: Kestrel Dravenmoor, a court translator who has spent a lifetime rendering other people's truths precisely, returns to the village of their childhood when the family house — sold without their knowledge by an aunt — goes to auction. The house holds the last living archive of Vessari, the dying language Kestrel's mother spoke only in whispers, and with it the answer to what really happened the night their father was taken away, a question the family's silence was built to protect. As bidders circle and relatives converge to perform a united grief they never felt, Kestrel begins translating the house itself: graffiti behind wallpaper, a ledger of borrowed words, a letter never posted. In the auction's final hour, Kestrel reads the letter aloud in Vessari before the assembled crowd, naming the uncle who informed on their father — an act of justice no court can now touch. They lose the house but leave owning the language, carrying it home word by word.
about_author: Ines Brightwater is the pen name of a former interpreter who spent eleven years in regional courts before turning to fiction. They write about the words families refuse to say and live near a coastline that is slowly being renamed.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Working in a sterile courtroom, Kestrel translates a stranger's testimony and realizes they've forgotten the Vessari word for 'father.' That night, a letter arrives: the childhood house will be auctioned in three weeks, listed by Aunt Maren. The beat is quiet dread — the inventory Kestrel keeps of unsaid things has just been foreclosed.

chapters.title: Everything the House Was Holding
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Arriving early, Kestrel searches the house ahead of the viewing and finds their mother's hidden word-ledger and, behind peeling wallpaper, names scratched into plaster — including their father's, dated the week he disappeared. Aunt Maren arrives unexpectedly; a brittle confrontation reveals she knows more than she'll say. The beat is excavation: memory surfacing like water through floorboards.

chapters.title: The Auction
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The whole family assembles to bid and to perform unity, while Uncle Aldous — charming, generous, the family's pillar — quietly outbids everyone. In the crowded rooms, Kestrel finds the unposted letter hidden in the ledger's binding: Aldous informed on their father, and Maren helped bury it. The climax builds as the gavel falls and Kestrel must choose between the inheritance of silence and the one of speech.

chapters.title: What Cannot Be Repossessed
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Before the new owners' movers arrive, Kestrel stands on the empty front step and reads the letter aloud in Vessari to the lingering crowd — naming Aldous, breaking the family's arrangement in the language meant to be forgotten. Aldous denies nothing; Maren finally weeps. Kestrel walks to the bus stop reciting the recovered words like a rosary. The beat is costly release: justice outside the law, belonging reclaimed in exile.
